questions.question: What's the difference between RSpec and Minitest in Rails?
questions.title: RSpec vs Minitest
questions.direct_answer: Minitest is Rails' default test framework: small, ships with Ruby, uses plain assert methods (assert_equal, assert_not). RSpec is a popular gem: a DSL with describe/it/expect syntax (expect(post).to be_valid) that many find more readable. Minitest files are test/models/post_test.rb with methods test 'name' do; RSpec files are spec/models/post_spec.rb with describe Post do; it '...' do. Both run the same assertions under the hood (Minitest assertions power RSpec's expectations). Choose: Minitest for zero-dependency simplicity and speed; RSpec for the expressive DSL and ecosystem (shoulda-matchers, FactoryBot). They're equivalent in power — it's a style choice, and you can even mix (spec with minitest assertions).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know Minitest is the default (assert_equal) and RSpec adds a DSL (describe/it/expect), and that they're a style choice.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking you MUST use RSpec (Minitest is fine), or mixing assertion styles chaotically in one suite.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Minitest = default, assert_equal (small, fast). RSpec = a gem, describe/it/expect DSL (readable). Both run the same assertions; it's a style choice.

sections.title: Default vs Expressive DSL
sections.content: Minitest is Rails' default test framework: small, ships with Ruby, uses plain assert methods (assert_equal, assert_not). RSpec is a popular gem: a DSL with describe, it, and expect syntax (expect post to be valid) that many find more readable. Minitest files are test slash models slash post_test dot rb with methods test name do; RSpec files are spec slash models slash post_spec dot rb with describe Post do; it do. Both run the same assertions under the hood (Minitest assertions power RSpec's expectations). Choose: Minitest for zero-dependency simplicity and speed; RSpec for the expressive DSL and ecosystem like shoulda-matchers and FactoryBot. They're equivalent in power — it's a style choice, and you can even mix spec with minitest assertions.

sections.title: Two Styles
sections.content:
Minitest: default, assert_equal, test/ files. RSpec: gem, describe/it/expect, spec/ files. Same assertions; style choice.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M[Minitest: default] --> A[assert_equal]
  R[RSpec: gem] --> E[describe/it/expect]
  A --> S[same assertions under the hood]
  E --> S
```

sections.title: RSpec vs Minitest
sections.content:
```ruby
# Minitest (DEFAULT; ships with Rails) — test/models/post_test.rb
class PostTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  test 'title is required' do
    p = Post.new(title: '')
    assert_not p.valid?            # plain assert
    assert p.errors[:title].any?
  end
end
# Run:  rails test

# RSpec (gem: gem 'rspec-rails') — spec/models/post_spec.rb
RSpec.describe Post, type: :model do
  it 'requires a title' do
    p = Post.new(title: '')
    expect(p).not_to be_valid       # expect DSL
    expect(p.errors[:title]).to be_present
  end
end
# Run:  rspec
# (with shoulda-matchers: it { should validate_presence_of(:title) })

# Both run the SAME assertions under the hood (Minitest powers RSpec).
# It's a style choice: assert (small/fast) vs expect (expressive DSL).
# Files: test/ (Minitest) vs spec/ (RSpec); run: rails test vs rspec.
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Thinking you MUST use RSpec — Minitest is fine and the default.
Mixing assertion styles chaotically in one suite (pick one).
Adding RSpec's weight when Minitest's simplicity would do.
